paragraphs: The Irish health service may spend €1 billion more than its budget this year, says the Parliamentary Budget Office. By the end of September, the HSE was already €781 million over budget. This is 8.6 per cent more than at the same time last year, but its budget went up by 5 per cent.

This was the first year that money went to six new health regions. Each region had to look after its own budget. But in September, four of the six regions lost the right to control their daily spending because they spent too much.

Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said the main problems are the cost of paying staff and the higher price of medicines. The plan was to hire about 3,300 workers in the second half of the year, but only if the service paid less for extra hours and agency staff. Instead, it hired about 3,600 people in the first half and did not save that money.

Experts say the health service needs budgets that are more real and that plan for several years. One expert said regions that stay inside their budget should get a reward. He also wants more care in local services, which cost less than hospitals. Next year health will get €29.1 billion, but some politicians think much of this new money will go to paying for this year's problem.

The Irish health service could overspend its budget by €1 billion this year, according to the Parliamentary Budget Office. By the end of September, the HSE's deficit had already reached €781 million, 8.6 per cent higher than at the same point last year, even though its budget rose by 5 per cent.

This year was the first in which funding was handed to six new health regions, each responsible for its own budget. However, in September four of the six regions lost their power to control day-to-day spending after running over budget.

Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill said the main causes are the pay bill and the rising cost of medicines. The service had planned to hire about 3,300 staff in the second half of the year if it reduced overtime and agency spending. Instead, it recruited around 3,600 people in the first half without making those savings.

Experts say the system needs more realistic budgets that plan over several years. One economist suggested rewarding regions that stay within budget and moving more care from hospitals to cheaper community services. Next year health will receive €29.1 billion, but opposition parties fear much of the increase will simply cover this year's gap.

Ireland's health service is on course to exceed its budget by €1 billion this year, the Parliamentary Budget Office has warned. By the end of September, the HSE's deficit had already climbed to €781 million, 8.6 per cent above the equivalent point last year, despite a 5 per cent boost to its allocation.

This year marked the first time that funding was devolved to six newly created health regions, each accountable for its own finances. In September, however, four of the six were stripped of their authority over day-to-day spending after overshooting their budgets.

Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill attributed the shortfall chiefly to the pay bill and soaring drug costs. Provision had been made for roughly 3,300 recruits in the second half of the year, on condition that overtime and agency spending were curbed. Instead, some 3,600 staff were taken on in the first half, with no corresponding savings.

Specialists argue that the system requires more credible, multiannual budgeting. One economist proposed rewarding regions that break even and shifting care away from hospitals towards less costly community services. Health is set to receive €29.1 billion next year, yet opposition parties fear that much of the uplift will merely plug this year's hole.

This year was the first in which funding was devolved to six newly established health regions, each accountable for its own expenditure. Nevertheless, in September four of the six regions were deprived of their authority over day-to-day spending after exceeding their budgets.

Health Minister Jennifer Carroll MacNeill attributed the deficit primarily to the pay bill and escalating pharmaceutical costs. Approximately 3,300 recruits had been budgeted for in the second half of the year, contingent upon reductions in overtime and agency expenditure. However, around 3,600 staff were recruited in the first half without any commensurate savings.

Analysts contend that the system requires more realistic, multiannual budgeting. One economist recommended incentivising regions that remain within budget and transferring care from hospitals to less expensive community services. Health is scheduled to receive €29.1 billion next year; consequently, opposition parties are concerned that a substantial proportion of the increase will merely offset this year's shortfall.
